groups.title: Cash
groups.summary: Sats a key can spend. Most outputs on chain are this.

groups.title: Objects
groups.summary: One sat that stands for a thing. Spending the sat moves the thing.

groups.title: Tokens
groups.summary: Token ledger entries: an inscription whose JSON names the amount (BSV-20, BSV-21), or a contract whose sats are the amount (STAS).

groups.title: Data
groups.summary: Records with no lock. They hold no value and can never be spent.

groups.title: Conditions
groups.summary: Locks that ask for more than one signature, for time to pass, or for nothing at all.

groups.title: Applications
groups.summary: Protocols that link many transactions into one structure: a tree of nodes, or a set of objects.

groups.title: Everything else
groups.summary: The catch-all for what has not been typed yet.

types.title: Pay to public key hash
types.summary: The ordinary payment. The lock names a key by its hash, and only that key can spend it.
description: A P2PKH output locks sats to the hash of a public key.
A Bitcoin address is that hash, written in Base58Check with a version byte in front.
To spend the output, the owner shows the full public key and signs the spending transaction with it.
history: P2PKH has been the standard payment since Bitcoin's first release in 2009.
Locking to a hash rather than the key itself keeps the key private until the first spend, and makes addresses shorter.
Wallets use it for payments and for change, so it is the most common output on chain by far.

spec.label: P2PKH on the Bitcoin SV wiki

parts.label: Copies the public key the spender supplies.
Hashes the copy with SHA-256, then RIPEMD-160.
20 bytes: the owner's key hash. This is the address.
Stops unless the two hashes match.
Checks the spender's signature against the key.

types.spend: A signature and the public key whose hash is in the lock: <signature> <public key>.

types.title: Pay to public key
types.summary: The first payment. The lock holds the public key itself, and only that key can spend it.
description: A P2PK output locks sats to a whole public key, with no hash in between.
To spend it, the owner signs the spending transaction with that key.
It has no address of its own, though tools often show the P2PKH address of the same key.
history: P2PK is the oldest payment on chain: the genesis coinbase and the coinbases of Bitcoin's first years pay this way.
P2PKH took over as the standard, because a hash is shorter to share and keeps the key private until the first spend.

parts.label: The owner's key: 65 bytes uncompressed, or 33 compressed.
Checks the spender's signature against the key.

types.spend: A signature from the key in the lock: <signature>.

types.title: Bare 1-sat output
types.summary: A P2PKH output holding exactly one sat, with no envelope. It may carry an object made earlier.
description: The lock is plain P2PKH; what makes it different is the amount.
Under the 1Sat Ordinals convention, a single sat can carry an inscription from the transaction that made it, through every transfer after.
So a 1-sat output with no envelope of its own may still be an object, and a careful wallet keeps it out of coin selection until it knows.
history: 1Sat Ordinals arrived on BSV in 2023, adapting the ordinal idea to whole outputs of one sat.
Wallets that follow it hold back every 1-sat output from payments, so an object is never spent as change by accident.

parts.label: The P2PKH opening.
20 bytes: the owner's key hash.
The P2PKH close.

pattern.note: The script is identical to P2PKH; the output's value is 1 sat.

types.spend: The owner's signature, as P2PKH. To move the object with it, send it on as 1 sat.

types.title: 1Sat Ordinals inscription
types.summary: A P2PKH lock plus an envelope that carries a file. The file is the object; the sat carries it.
description: An inscription puts a file inside the locking script, wrapped in an envelope that never runs.
The envelope opens with OP_FALSE OP_IF, so the script skips it, and names itself with the word "ord".
The output where the file first appears is its origin, and the origin outpoint is the object's id for life.
Each later spend of that single sat moves the object to a new owner.
history: Ordinal inscriptions began on BTC in early 2023.
1Sat Ordinals brought the envelope to BSV the same year, with one change that matters: an object is a whole 1-sat output, so tracking it needs no sat numbering.
Because BSV has no small data limit, the file can be a full image, page or program.

parts.label: A P2PKH lock: who owns the object.
Opens the envelope. The script never runs what follows.
Names the envelope as an inscription.
Field 1: the file's media type, such as image/png.
Field 0: the file itself.
Closes the envelope.

pattern.note: Some inscriptions put the envelope before the lock instead of after it.

types.spend: The owner's signature, as P2PKH, sent on as 1 sat so the object goes with it.

types.title: Inscription with MAP
types.summary: An inscription with a MAP tail after the lock, naming the object's fields.
description: The same envelope and lock as any inscription, followed by OP_RETURN and a MAP record.
The MAP record holds key-value pairs about the object, such as its name, its collection or its traits.
Everything after OP_RETURN is data, so the tail never affects who can spend the output.
history: Collections minted on 1Sat Ordinals commonly use a MAP tail to carry names and traits beside the file.

parts.label: A P2PKH lock: who owns the object.
The inscription envelope.
Ends the script. What follows is data.
The MAP prefix.
The object's fields, as pairs.

types.spend: The owner's signature, as P2PKH.

types.title: OrdLock listing
types.summary: An object offered for sale. The lock itself is the offer: it names the price and who gets paid.
description: OrdLock is a contract that holds an object until someone pays for it.
The seller writes the payment they want, as a whole output, into the lock.
Any buyer can open it by building a transaction that includes that exact output, so the seller is paid in the same transaction that hands over the object, or neither happens.
The seller can also cancel with a signature.
history: OrdLock came with the 1Sat Ordinals marketplace in 2023, so listings could live on chain rather than in a market's database.
It ships in the @1sat/templates package that wallets use to build and read listings.

parts.label: Fixed contract code that checks the spending transaction.
20 bytes: who can cancel.
The output a buyer must create: the price in sats and the seller's lock.
More fixed contract code.

pattern.note: The contract code is the same in every listing; only the seller and the payout change.

types.spend: Either the seller cancels with a signature, or anyone buys by paying the price the lock names.

types.title: BSV-20
types.summary: Fungible tokens named by ticker, written as JSON inscriptions. First deploy of a ticker wins.
description: A BSV-20 token is a run of inscriptions with the content type application/bsv-20.
A deploy names a ticker and sets its maximum supply and the most any one mint may claim.
Mints claim amounts until the supply runs out, and transfers move amounts between owners.
Balances come from an indexer that replays every operation in order and applies the rules: the first deploy of a ticker counts, and later ones are ignored.
history: BSV-20 launched on 1Sat Ordinals in 2023, after the BRC-20 experiment on BTC.
Open minting by ticker made launches fair, but meant every indexer had to scan every mint to know a balance.
BSV-21 followed to fix that, and is the format new tokens use.

parts.label: A P2PKH lock: who holds the tokens.
Opens the inscription envelope.
The content type that marks a token operation.
The operation: deploy, mint or transfer, by ticker.
Closes the envelope.

types.spend: The owner's signature, as P2PKH. A transfer must account for the whole amount it spends.

types.title: BSV-21
types.summary: Fungible tokens with no ticker race. One output creates the token and its whole supply, and its outpoint is the token's id.
description: A BSV-21 token starts with a single deploy+mint inscription that creates the whole supply at once.
The token's id is that output's outpoint, written as txid_vout.
Every transfer names the id, so any indexer can check a balance by following outputs back to the genesis, without scanning every mint on chain.
The issuer decides how the supply is handed out, for example through a contract that releases it over time.
history: BSV-21 came to 1Sat Ordinals in late 2023 as the successor to BSV-20.
Ids replaced tickers, so two tokens may share a symbol and still never collide.
Stablecoins such as MNEE use it.

parts.label: A P2PKH lock: who holds the tokens.
Opens the inscription envelope.
The same content type as BSV-20.
A genesis. A transfer instead carries "op":"transfer" and the token's "id".
Closes the envelope.

types.spend: The owner's signature, as P2PKH. A transfer must account for the whole amount it spends.

types.title: OP_RETURN data
types.summary: Data with no lock. Anything at all can follow it; nothing on chain says how to read it.
description: An output that starts with OP_FALSE OP_RETURN can never be spent, so it is a safe place to write data.
Nodes know it can never be spent and can leave it out of the set of coins they track.
Protocols such as B, MAP and AIP give the data a shape by starting it with a known prefix.
history: Bitcoin made small OP_RETURN outputs standard in 2014, so people would stop hiding data in fake addresses.
BSV later lifted the size limit, which made whole files on chain practical.
A plain OP_RETURN before OP_FALSE was added could be spent in some cases; OP_FALSE OP_RETURN rules that out.

spec.label: OP_RETURN on the Bitcoin SV wiki

parts.label: Puts false on the stack, so the output can never be spent.
Ends the script. What follows is data.
Any number of pushes, in any format.

types.spend: It cannot be spent. Any sats sent to it are gone for good.

types.title: B:// file
types.summary: A file on chain: the data, its media type, its encoding and an optional name, under the B prefix.
description: B is a Bitcom protocol for storing a file in an OP_RETURN output.
Its prefix is a Bitcoin address, 19HxigV4QyBv3tHpQVcUEQyq1pzZVdoAut, and the fields after it are fixed in order.
Any page or app can then load the file by its transaction id.
history: unwriter published B in 2019 as one of the first Bitcom protocols, alongside tools that served B files straight to the browser.
It became the common way to put images, pages and media on chain, and other protocols pipe into it.

parts.label: A data output.
The B prefix.
The file's bytes.
Such as image/png or text/markdown.
Such as binary or utf-8.
Optional.
Optional: a pipe, then another protocol such as MAP or AIP.

types.spend: It cannot be spent.

explore.label: See B in the Bitcom registry

types.title: MAP record
types.summary: Key-value pairs that say what a transaction is for: its app, its type, and any fields the app needs.
description: MAP, the Magic Attribute Protocol, writes pairs of keys and values into an OP_RETURN output.
A SET command adds pairs; apps use them to label a post, a like, a ticket or an object.
Because MAP is a Bitcom protocol, it can follow another one in the same output after a pipe.
history: MAP was published in 2019 and became the shared vocabulary of many BSV apps.
Its keys are free-form, so each app documents its own and readers agree on the common ones, such as app and type.

parts.label: A data output.
The MAP prefix.
The command.
Pairs, such as app and type.

types.spend: It cannot be spent.

explore.label: See MAP in the Bitcom registry

types.title: AIP signature
types.summary: A signature over the data before it, so a record names its author.
description: AIP, the Author Identity Protocol, signs the fields that come before it in the same output.
It records the signing method, the signer's address and the signature, and may list which fields it covers.
Anyone can check the signature without trusting the app that wrote it.
history: AIP was published in 2019 and is often piped after B and MAP, so a post carries its file, its labels and its author together.

parts.label: Usually follows other data, after a pipe.
The AIP prefix.
The signing method.
The signer's address.
The signature over the covered fields.
Optional: which fields the signature covers.

types.spend: It cannot be spent.

explore.label: See AIP in the Bitcom registry

types.title: SIGMA signature
types.summary: A signature over a record and the transaction's inputs, so it cannot be copied into another transaction.
description: SIGMA signs the data before it together with an input of the transaction that carries it.
That ties the signature to this one transaction, so nobody can lift it into a different one and claim the author's name.
Like AIP, it follows other data after a pipe.
history: SIGMA came from the Bitcoin Schema project as a successor to AIP for signing on-chain records.

parts.label: Follows other data, such as MAP, after a pipe.
The SIGMA prefix.
The signing method: a Bitcoin signed message.
The signer's address.
The signature.
Which input the signature is bound to.

types.spend: It cannot be spent.

types.title: Pay to script hash
types.summary: Locks to the hash of a script, which the spender reveals. Retired from Bitcoin at the Genesis upgrade.
description: A P2SH output holds the hash of a script, not the script itself.
From 2012, a spender showed the matching script and met its conditions, and nodes ran that script as an extra step.
Since the Genesis upgrade in 2020, nodes no longer take that extra step for new outputs, so this shape only checks the hash.
history: BIP 16 added P2SH in 2012, so that multisig and other long scripts could fit behind a short address.
Genesis restored the original script rules at block 620,538, and P2SH was retired with that change.
Outputs created before Genesis still spend by the old rule.

parts.label: Hashes the script the spender supplies.
20 bytes: the hash the script must match.
Succeeds only when the two hashes match.

types.spend: Before Genesis: the script's own unlock data, then the script. After it: the bytes that hash to the value in the lock.

types.title: Bare multisig
types.summary: Lists several keys and asks for a number of them to sign, such as any two of three.
description: A bare multisig output writes every public key into the lock, then the number of signatures it needs.
It suits shared funds and escrow, where no single key holder should be able to spend alone.
Bare means the keys sit in the lock itself, not behind a hash.
history: OP_CHECKMULTISIG has been part of Bitcoin's script since the start.
An off-by-one in it consumes one extra stack item, which is why every unlock starts with OP_0.

spec.label: Multisignature on the Bitcoin SV wiki

parts.label: How many signatures are needed (m).
Every key that may sign, 33 bytes each.
How many keys there are (n).
Checks the signatures against the keys, in order.

pattern.note: Shown as 2-of-3; m and n can be anything up to 16.

types.spend: OP_0, then m signatures in the same order as their keys.

types.title: Cosign
types.summary: The owner signs, then a named cosigner. A service can approve each transfer without ever holding the funds.
description: A cosign lock is P2PKH for the owner, followed by a second check against one fixed public key.
The owner cannot move the output alone, and the cosigner cannot move it at all without the owner.
Token issuers use it so their service can apply rules to each transfer.
history: Cosign ships in @1sat/templates.
The MNEE stablecoin uses it, so each MNEE transfer carries the issuer's approval.

parts.label: Checks the owner's key, as P2PKH does.
Checks the owner's signature, and stops if it fails.
33 bytes: the cosigner's key.
Checks the cosigner's signature.

types.spend: The cosigner's signature, then the owner's signature and public key: <cosigner sig> <owner sig> <owner pubkey>.

types.title: Time lock
types.summary: Sats the owner cannot move until a chosen block height.
description: A time lock is a contract that checks the spending transaction's lock time against a block height written into the output.
Until the chain reaches that height, no transaction can spend it, not even the owner's.
After that, the owner spends it with a signature.
history: Locking coins to show commitment, for example to back a post or a vote, became popular on BSV in 2023.
This contract ships in @1sat/templates.

parts.label: Fixed contract code that reads the spending transaction.
20 bytes: who may spend after the lock ends.
The height the chain must reach first.
More fixed contract code.

types.spend: The owner's signature, in a transaction the chain accepts only once the block height is reached.

types.title: Transaction lock time
types.summary: A transaction no block may include until a chosen block height or time has passed.
description: Every transaction ends with a lock time field, and most leave it at 0.
A nonzero lock time below 500,000,000 is a block height; from 500,000,000 on it is a unix time.
The lock binds only when at least one input's sequence number is below 0xffffffff.
When every input is final, the rules ignore the lock time.

Many wallets set a binding lock time just below the current height on every payment, to discourage miners from rewriting recent blocks (anti-fee-sniping); the next block already meets it, so nobody waits on it.
So Bitblocks types a transaction nlocktime only when its lock binds and sits more than 2,016 blocks (or 14 days, two weeks) before the block it was mined in.
This lock belongs to the whole transaction, not to one output: it says when the transaction itself becomes valid.
history: Lock time is in the first Bitcoin release, as the way to replace a transaction before it is final.

From 2015, Bitcoin Core set it to the current height with a sequence of 0xfffffffe on every payment, so many transactions from those years carry one; the transaction page shows it, labelled anti-fee-sniping, and these are not this type.

parts.label: At least one input with a sequence below 0xffffffff.
Any outputs.
4 bytes: a block height below 500,000,000, else a unix time.

pattern.note: A nonzero lock time with every sequence at 0xffffffff is ignored, and is not this type.

types.spend: Its outputs are spent as their own scripts say; the lock only decides when the transaction can be mined.

types.title: Anyone can spend
types.summary: OP_TRUE and nothing else. Whoever sees it first can take it.
description: The lock is a single OP_TRUE, which always succeeds, so spending it needs no signature at all.
Sats sent here belong to whoever spends them first, usually a bot or a miner.
People use it for puzzles, tests and giveaways, and sometimes by mistake.
history: Anyone-can-spend outputs are as old as Bitcoin's script.

spec.label: Script on the Bitcoin SV wiki

parts.label: Leaves true on the stack. The output is unlocked.

types.spend: Nothing. An empty unlocking script will do.

types.title: Metanet node
types.summary: A transaction that is a node in a tree of on-chain content, linked to its parent by the parent's signature.
description: The Metanet structures data on chain as a directed graph, so content in different transactions can be related, named and found.
A node is a transaction with an OP_RETURN output that starts with the four-byte Metanet flag, "meta", followed by the node's public key and its parent's transaction id.
An edge from parent to child exists only when the parent's key signs an input of the child, so only a parent can add children.
Nobody needs to trust an index: anyone can rebuild the whole graph from the chain.
history: nChain proposed the Metanet as a layer on the blockchain that needs no change to the protocol or its consensus rules.
Its technical summary describes how nodes, edges, versions and names give the chain the shape of an internet, with resource locators like URLs.
Bitblocks detects Metanet nodes as they sync, and the Metanet explorer walks their trees.

parts.label: The parent's signature and key. This is what creates the edge.
A data output.
The Metanet flag: this transaction is a node.
The node's public key: its address.
The parent's transaction id. Without it, the node is a root.
Optional: a name, keywords, a file and its type.

pattern.note: The node's id is H(P_node || TxID_node): its key and its own transaction id, hashed together.

types.spend: The node's OP_RETURN output cannot be spent. Its key, P_node, signs for the node's children in later transactions.

concepts.text: A transaction carrying the Metanet flag. It stores content, and it has a public key, P_node, written in its OP_RETURN. Its id is the hash of that key and its transaction id.

A link from a parent to a child. It exists only when the parent's key signs an input of the child, so a parent alone decides its children. A node has at most one parent and may have any number of children. An edge is a logical link: the child need not spend an output of the parent.
A node with no parent, or whose parent field does not point to a valid Metanet node. A root is like a top-level domain; its children are sub-domains, and a node with no children is an end point.
Two nodes with the same public key are versions of one node. The one with the most proof of work behind it is the latest: the higher block, or within a block, the later transaction.
A Metanet URL, built like a web address from a domain name, a path and a file: mnp://bobsblog/path/file. Each part maps to a node in the tree.

A node's fixed attributes are its id and its parent's id; a name and keywords are optional. An explorer finds every transaction with the flag, checks it is a valid node, and indexes its keywords. A node may also carry a hash of its content, so it can be found by what it holds.

Content can go in one OP_RETURN after the node fields; in an OP_RETURN header followed by pushes that are dropped with OP_DROP; or across several sibling transactions that share a parent and carry an index for reassembly.

attribution.text: The summary and concepts on this page are adapted from The Metanet Technical Summary, original work by nChain Limited.
attribution.share_alike: This adaptation is shared under the same licence.

types.title: Run jig
types.summary: A JavaScript object that lives on chain. Each update is a transaction, and its owner is whoever holds its output.
description: Run is a protocol for tokens and objects written as JavaScript classes, called jigs.
Each transaction carries a Run record in OP_RETURN that says which jigs it creates or updates, and outputs that hold each jig's current owner.
A Run client replays the record to rebuild each jig's state, so the chain is the database.
history: Run launched on BSV in 2020 and hosted NFT collections and games, among them the Rexxies.
Bitblocks traces the Rexxies collection through its Run jigs.

parts.label: A data output.
The Run prefix.
The protocol version.
The app that wrote it.
JSON: the jigs this transaction creates or updates, and how.

pattern.note: Each jig's owner is a separate output, usually P2PKH.

types.spend: The Run record cannot be spent. Each jig moves when its owner spends the output that holds it.

types.title: STAS token
types.summary: A token whose amount is the output's sats, held by a contract that keeps it a token on every spend.
description: A STAS output starts as a P2PKH lock: the owner's pubkey hash.
A fixed contract follows that reads the spending transaction, so the sats can only move on to outputs with the same contract and the same token.
After OP_RETURN come the token's data: the issuer's redemption pubkey hash, which is the token's id, a flag byte (00 splittable, 01 not), then the symbol and any other data.
Each satoshi is one unit of the token, so the amount is the output's value.
history: TAAL published STAS with the stas-js library and a white paper in 2021.
The tokens WhatsOnChain lists were issued from September 2021, around block 706,000.

parts.token: OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <owner pubkey hash> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG
parts.label: A P2PKH lock: who holds the tokens.
1,384 bytes of fixed contract code that checks the spending transaction's outputs.
20 bytes: the issuer's key, and the token's id.
One byte: 00 when the token may be split, 01 when it may not.
What the issuer wrote, such as the symbol.

pattern.note: The contract is the same byte for byte in every STAS output; only the owner and the token data change.

types.spend: The owner's signature, in a transaction whose outputs carry the same STAS contract and token data on to the next owners, or back to the issuer to redeem.

types.title: HodLocker post or like
types.summary: A post or a like backed by sats in a time lock. The lock is the vote: what it holds, and for how long.
description: HodLocker was a social app where people locked sats to what they wrote and to what they liked.
A post is a time lock output, then a B record with the text and a MAP record with app hodlocker.com, type post and the author's paymail.
A reply is a post whose MAP record also names the post it answers, as context tx and tx.
A like is a time lock output, then a MAP record with type like and the txid of the post it backs.
Nothing can move the locked sats before the unlock height; after it, the owner spends them with a signature.
history: HodLocker ran on BSV from 2023; the posts Bitblocks has read date from September 2023 to March 2024, around blocks 810,000 to 838,000.
Its source is public at github.com/zer0dt/hodlocker; hodlocker.com no longer serves the app.

parts.label: The sats locked, the owner, and the unlock height.
A post's text, as a B record. A like has none.

parts.token: MAP SET app hodlocker.com type post
parts.label: Or type like, with tx <txid>: the post the lock backs.

pattern.note: A reply's MAP record adds context tx and tx <txid>, the post it answers.

types.spend: The locked output, by its owner's signature from the unlock height on. The data output cannot be spent.

types.title: Custom
types.summary: Any output that matches none of the types above. Its count is the measure of what is left to type.
description: Custom is not a format.
It is where an output lands when its script matches no type we have defined yet.
Some are one-off contracts, some are protocols we have not written up, and some are mistakes.
As we add types, the custom count goes down.
history: Typing every output on chain is ongoing work, tracked in the open.

parts.label: Anything not matched by another type.

types.spend: Depends on the script. Some can be spent; some never can.
